## Today

::: {.paradigm}
[Internal state]{.pbox}
[Motion capacity]{.pbox .on}
[Navigation capacity]{.pbox .on}
[External factors]{.pbox}
[Movement path]{.pbox .path .on}
:::

Random walks are the simplest possible answers to *how* an animal moves and
*where* it is heading. Their value is not realism — it is that they tell you
what to expect **if nothing else were going on**.

---

## Where we are going

::: {.objectives}
1. Why simulate: you cannot rewind an animal, but you can simulate a null
2. The uncorrelated random walk and mean squared displacement
3. Correlated random walks: persistence, and the scales of movement
4. Biased random walks: advection versus diffusion
5. Lévy walks — and an honest account of the controversy
6. Using simulations as hypothesis tests
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Today's practical builds a simulator from scratch. The same simulated animal
becomes the **ground truth** you test estimators against in Sessions 6 and 7.
:::

# 1 · Why model movement? {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## You cannot rewind an animal

::: {.incremental}
- A tracking study observes **one realisation** of a random process
- To ask "is this unusual?" you need the distribution of what *could* have
  happened — and nature will not rerun the experiment
- A movement model is a recipe that **generates** tracks. Run it a thousand
  times and you have that distribution
- Compare the real track with the simulated ones: where does it fall?
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
A random walk is a **null model**. When the animal departs from it, the
departure is the biology: memory, attraction, avoidance, a home range.
:::

---

## Four canonical walks

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| fig-align: center
source("R/simulators.R")
set.seed(3)
n <- 400
rw   <- simulate_crw(n, kappa = 0)
crw  <- simulate_crw(n, kappa = 4)
bcrw <- simulate_bcrw(n, goal = c(25000, 0), w = 0.3, kappa = 4, start = c(0, 0))
lsl  <- pmin(50 * runif(n)^(-1 / 1.1), 15000)            # Pareto, mu = 2.1
lh   <- runif(n, -pi, pi)
levy <- data.frame(x = cumsum(lsl * cos(lh)), y = cumsum(lsl * sin(lh)))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 3, 0.5))
for (d in list(list(rw, "Random walk"), list(crw, "Correlated (κ = 4)"),
               list(bcrw, "Biased correlated"), list(levy, "Lévy walk (μ ≈ 2)"))) {
  plot(d[[1]]$x, d[[1]]$y, type = "l", asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 1.2)
  points(0, 0, pch = 17, col = "firebrick", cex = 1.6)
  if (d[[2]] == "Biased correlated") points(25000, 0, pch = 4, col = "firebrick", cex = 2, lwd = 3)
  title(d[[2]], cex.main = 2)
}
par(op)
```

[Figure produced with own R code · simulated data]{.credit}


Same number of steps. Red triangle: start. Cross: the goal of the biased walk.

# 2 · The uncorrelated random walk {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## The Brownian baseline

::: {.incremental}
- Each step has a random length and a **uniformly random** direction,
  independent of the previous one
- The animal has no memory and no goal
- After $n$ steps the expected squared distance from the start — the **mean
  squared displacement** — is
  $$\text{MSD}(n) = n\,\mathrm{E}[l^2]$$
- MSD grows **linearly** with time: $\text{MSD} = 4Dt$ in two dimensions, with
  $D$ the diffusion coefficient
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Linear MSD means the typical distance from the start grows only as
$\sqrt{t}$. A random walker four times as long gets only twice as far.
:::

---

## Diffusion, seen from above

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(10)
walks <- lapply(1:300, function(i) simulate_crw(1000, kappa = 0))
el2   <- 2 * 3 * 250^2                     # E[l²] for gamma(shape 2, scale 250)
at    <- c(10, 100, 1000)
cols  <- c(rust, gold, teal)

layout(matrix(1:2, 1), widths = c(1, 1.2))
map_par()
lim <- c(-1, 1) * 2.6 * sqrt(1000 * el2) / 1000
plot(NA, xlim = lim, ylim = lim, asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     main = "300 walkers after 10, 100, 1000 steps")
for (k in 3:1) {
  p <- t(sapply(walks, function(w) unlist(w[at[k], c("x", "y")]))) / 1000
  points(p, pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = adjustcolor(cols[k], 0.6))
  symbols(0, 0, circles = sqrt(at[k] * el2) / 1000, inches = FALSE, add = TRUE,
          fg = cols[k], lwd = 3)
}
points(0, 0, pch = 17, cex = 1.6)
legend("bottomright", paste(at, "steps"), col = cols, pch = 16, bty = "n", cex = 1.3)
slide_par()
n_seq <- seq(10, 1000, by = 10)
msd_n <- sapply(n_seq, function(n) mean(sapply(walks, function(w) w$x[n]^2 + w$y[n]^2))) / 1e6
plot(n_seq, msd_n, pch = 16, col = teal, xlab = "Steps", ylab = "MSD (km²)",
     main = "MSD grows linearly")
abline(0, el2 / 1e6, lwd = 3, col = rust)
legend("topleft", c("simulated", "n E[l²]"), pch = c(16, NA), lty = c(NA, 1), lwd = 3,
       col = c(teal, rust), bty = "n", cex = 1.3)
```

[Figure produced with own R code · simulated data]{.credit}


Circles: the root of the expected MSD. Ten times more steps, only $\sqrt{10}
\approx 3.2$ times further.

# 3 · Correlated random walks {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Persistence

A **correlated random walk** (CRW) draws each new heading close to the last:

$$\phi_t = \phi_{t-1} + \theta_t, \qquad \theta_t \sim \text{von Mises}(0, \kappa)$$

::: {.incremental}
- $\kappa = 0$: turning angles uniform — the uncorrelated walk
- large $\kappa$: turning angles near zero — nearly straight lines
- Step lengths from a gamma, Weibull or log-normal distribution
- Two parameters for steps, one for turns: the same ingredients as the step
  selection functions of Session 7 and the hidden Markov models of Session 8
:::

---

## The two ingredients

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); slide_par()
sl <- seq(0, 2500, length.out = 400)
plot(NA, xlim = range(sl), ylim = c(0, 0.0021), yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Step length (m)", ylab = "Density", main = "Gamma steps, mean 500 m")
shapes <- c(1, 2, 5); scols <- c(gold, teal, rust)
for (i in 1:3) lines(sl, dgamma(sl, shape = shapes[i], scale = 500 / shapes[i]), lwd = 4, col = scols[i])
legend("topright", paste("shape =", shapes), col = scols, lwd = 4, bty = "n", cex = 1.3)

th <- seq(-pi, pi, length.out = 400)
kap <- c(0, 1, 4, 10); kcols <- c("grey50", gold, teal, rust)
plot(NA, xlim = c(-180, 180), ylim = c(0, 1.3), xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Turning angle (degrees)", ylab = "Density", main = "von Mises turns")
axis(1, at = seq(-180, 180, 90))
for (i in 1:4) lines(th * 180 / pi, exp(kap[i] * cos(th)) / (2 * pi * besselI(kap[i], 0)),
                     lwd = 4, col = kcols[i])
legend("topright", paste("κ =", kap), col = kcols, lwd = 4, bty = "n", cex = 1.3)
```

[Figure produced with own R code · theoretical distributions]{.credit}


Every random walk in this session, and every SSF and HMM later, is built
from one distribution of each kind.

---

## The scales of movement

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-align: center
source("R/simulators.R")
msd <- function(d, lags) sapply(lags, function(L)
  mean((d$x[-(1:L)] - head(d$x, -L))^2 + (d$y[-(1:L)] - head(d$y, -L))^2))
lags <- 2^(0:8)
set.seed(1)
cols <- c("grey40", "#1f6f78", "#c1440e")
curves <- lapply(c(0, 2, 10), function(k)
  rowMeans(sapply(1:30, function(j) msd(simulate_crw(2000, kappa = k), lags))))
op <- par(mar = c(4.5, 5, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = range(lags), ylim = range(unlist(curves)) * c(0.15, 2), log = "xy",
     xlab = "Lag (steps)", ylab = "Mean squared displacement (m²)",
     cex.lab = 1.5, cex.axis = 1.3)
for (i in 1:3) {
  lines(lags, curves[[i]], col = cols[i], lwd = 3)
  points(lags, curves[[i]], col = cols[i], pch = 16, cex = 1.3)
}
# guides: slope 2 under kappa = 10 at short lags; slope 1 under kappa = 0 at long lags
s2 <- lags[1:5];  lines(s2, 0.35 * curves[[3]][1] * s2^2, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
s1 <- lags[5:9];  lines(s1, 0.35 * curves[[1]][9] * s1 / lags[9], lty = 3, lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", c("κ = 0", "κ = 2", "κ = 10", "slope 2: ballistic", "slope 1: diffusive"),
       col = c(cols, "black", "black"), lwd = c(3, 3, 3, 2, 2), lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 3),
       bty = "n", cex = 1.3)
par(op)
```

[Figure produced with own R code · simulated data]{.credit}


Short lags: persistence makes a CRW **ballistic** (MSD ∝ t²). Long lags: it
forgets its direction and becomes **diffusive** (MSD ∝ t). The crossover is
the scale of the animal's directional memory.

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
You plot MSD against lag on log–log axes for a real track. The slope is ~1.8
at lags up to 3 hours, then ~1.0 up to 10 days, then **flattens to ~0**. What
does each regime suggest?

- [ ] Nothing — MSD is always linear for real animals
- [x] Directed movement at short scales, random-walk-like at intermediate scales, and confinement to a home range at long scales
- [ ] GPS error at short scales, directed movement at long scales
- [ ] The track needs resampling

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Slope near 2: ballistic, persistent movement — the animal keeps its heading
for a few hours. Slope near 1: diffusive, a correlated random walk has
forgotten its direction. Slope near 0: MSD stops growing because the animal
cannot get any further from where it was — a **home range**.

That last regime is what an unbiased random walk can never produce, and it is
the starting point of Session 6. One caution: very short lags can also look
flat because GPS error sets a floor on the smallest measurable displacement.
:::
:::

# 4 · Biased random walks {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Advection and diffusion

Add a preferred direction — towards a den, a water hole, a breeding ground:

::: {.incremental}
- **Biased random walk (BRW)**: each heading drawn around the bearing to the
  goal, with no memory of the last heading
- **Biased correlated random walk (BCRW)**: a compromise between the previous
  heading (persistence) and the bearing to the goal (bias)
- Two processes act at once: **advection** (drift towards the goal, distance
  ∝ $t$) and **diffusion** (random spread, distance ∝ $\sqrt{t}$)
- Over long enough times, advection always wins
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
Weak bias is invisible over a few steps and decisive over many. That is why
orientation mechanisms are so hard to detect in short tracks and so obvious in
migrations.
:::

---

## Drift beats spread, eventually

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| cache: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(12)
goal <- c(1e8, 0)                                   # far to the east: a fixed bearing
reps <- lapply(1:120, function(i) simulate_bcrw(600, goal = goal, w = 0.1, kappa = 2,
                                                start = c(0, 0), heading0 = runif(1, -pi, pi)))
X <- sapply(reps, `[[`, "x") / 1000; Y <- sapply(reps, `[[`, "y") / 1000

layout(matrix(1:2, 1), widths = c(1.2, 1))
map_par()
plot(NA, xlim = range(X[, 1:25]), ylim = range(Y[, 1:25]), asp = 1, axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "25 walkers, weak bias to the east")
for (j in 1:25) lines(X[, j], Y[, j], col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.5))
points(0, 0, pch = 17, cex = 1.6, col = rust)
slide_par()
drift  <- rowMeans(X)
spread <- apply(Y, 1, sd)
plot(1:600, drift, type = "l", lwd = 4, col = rust, ylim = c(0, max(drift, spread)),
     xlab = "Steps", ylab = "km", main = "Advection vs diffusion")
lines(1:600, spread, lwd = 4, col = teal)
cross <- which(drift > spread)[1]
abline(v = cross, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", c("mean progress east: grows like t", "sideways spread: grows like √t"),
       col = c(rust, teal), lwd = 4, bty = "n", cex = 1.3)
```

[Figure produced with own R code · simulated data]{.credit}


A weak pull towards the east (bias weight 0.1). For the first
`r round(cross, -1)` steps the random spread is larger than the progress;
after that, drift wins for good.

---

## Central places

A BCRW whose goal is its own **home** produces something new: the animal
wanders, drifts back, wanders again. It never escapes.

::: {.incremental}
- The track stays within a bounded area: a **home range** emerges from a simple
  movement rule
- The long-run spread of positions is a stationary **utilisation distribution**
- Mechanistic home-range models (Moorcroft & Lewis 2006) build on exactly this
  idea
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
In the practical this central-place walker becomes our **ground-truth
animal**: we know its true home range, so in Session 6 we can check which
estimator gets it right.
:::

---

## A home range from one rule

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| cache: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-align: center
truth <- truth_animal()
set.seed(5)
long <- do.call(simulate_bcrw, c(list(n = 60000), truth_rule))
kd   <- MASS::kde2d(long$x / 1000, long$y / 1000, n = 150, lims = c(-25, 25, -25, 25))
lev  <- sort(kd$z, decreasing = TRUE)
c95  <- lev[which(cumsum(lev) / sum(lev) >= 0.95)[1]]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); map_par()
plot(truth$x / 1000, truth$y / 1000, type = "l", asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.6), xlim = c(-25, 25), ylim = c(-25, 25),
     main = "5,000 steps of the ground-truth animal")
points(0, 0, pch = 17, cex = 1.8, col = rust)
scale_bar(10, unit = 1)
z <- kd$z; z[z < max(z) * 0.01] <- NA
image(kd$x, kd$y, z, col = hcl.colors(60, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE), asp = 1, axes = FALSE,
      xlab = "", ylab = "", xlim = c(-25, 25), ylim = c(-25, 25),
      main = "Its long-run UD (60,000 steps)")
contour(kd$x, kd$y, kd$z, levels = c95, drawlabels = FALSE, add = TRUE, lwd = 3, lty = 2)
points(0, 0, pch = 17, cex = 1.8, col = rust)
```

[Figure produced with own R code · simulated data]{.credit}


No memory, no map, no boundary — only a weak pull towards home. Dashed: the
true 95% range, about 800 km², which Session 6 tries to recover.

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
A homing pigeon is simulated as a BCRW with a weak bias towards its loft. Over
the first 10 steps its track is indistinguishable from an unbiased CRW. Over
500 steps it heads unmistakably home. Why?

- [ ] The bias strength increases with time
- [x] Drift accumulates linearly with time while random spread grows only with its square root
- [ ] The CRW component weakens over time
- [ ] Simulation error

::: {.quiz-feedback}
The bias adds a small, consistent component to every step: after $n$ steps
the drift has accumulated in proportion to $n$. The random component partly
cancels itself out, growing only as $\sqrt{n}$. Eventually the drift must
dominate.

Detecting orientation in real animals is hard for exactly this reason: over a
short track, even a genuine bias is swamped by noise.
:::
:::

# 5 · Lévy walks {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## The Lévy hypothesis

::: {.incremental}
- Step lengths drawn from a **power law**: $P(l) \propto l^{-\mu}$, with
  $1 < \mu \le 3$
- No characteristic scale: many short steps, occasional enormous ones
- Viswanathan et al. (1996) reported Lévy flights in wandering albatrosses;
  Viswanathan et al. (1999) showed that $\mu \approx 2$ is an **optimal search**
  strategy for sparse, randomly placed targets
- A seductive idea: a universal, scale-free rule for foraging
:::

---

## The reversal

::: {.incremental}
- Edwards et al. (2007) reanalysed the albatross data with better records:
  the long "flights" included time sitting on the water. **The Lévy pattern
  disappeared**
- They also showed that log–log regression of histograms, the standard method
  at the time, is biased; power laws must be fitted by **maximum likelihood**
  and compared with alternatives (Clauset et al. 2009)
- Benhamou (2007): an animal **switching between two behaviours**, each a
  simple random walk, produces a step-length distribution that a power law
  fits beautifully
- Lévy-like patterns do appear in some marine predators, but depend on
  environmental context (Sims et al. 2008; Humphries et al. 2010)
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
The honest position: a power-law fit is not evidence of a Lévy *strategy*.
Different mechanisms produce indistinguishable step-length distributions.
:::

---

## Two ways to make a heavy tail

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(4)
samples <- list(
  "exponential"           = rexp(2000, 1 / 300) + 50,
  "power law, μ = 2"      = 50 * runif(2000)^(-1),
  "two exponential modes" = c(rexp(1500, 1 / 60), rexp(500, 1 / 1500)) + 10)
tcols <- c("grey50", gold, rust)

layout(matrix(1:2, 1), widths = c(1.1, 1))
slide_par()
plot(NA, xlim = c(10, 2e5), ylim = c(5e-4, 1), log = "xy", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Step length l (m)", ylab = "P(step > l)", main = "Tails on log–log axes")
axis(1, at = 10^(1:5), labels = c("10", "100", "1 km", "10 km", "100 km"))
axis(2, at = 10^(0:-3), labels = c("1", "0.1", "0.01", "0.001"))
for (i in 1:3) {
  x <- sort(samples[[i]])
  lines(x, 1 - (seq_along(x) - 1) / length(x), lwd = 4, col = tcols[i])
}
legend("bottomleft", names(samples), col = tcols, lwd = 4, bty = "n", cex = 1.3)

# a composite walk: switching between searching and travelling
n <- 600; state <- integer(n); state[1] <- 1
for (i in 2:n) state[i] <- if (runif(1) < c(0.04, 0.2)[state[i - 1]]) 3 - state[i - 1] else state[i - 1]
sl <- rexp(n, 1 / c(60, 1500)[state])
hd <- cumsum(ifelse(state == 1, runif(n, -pi, pi), rvm(n, 0, 6)))
x <- cumsum(sl * cos(hd)) / 1000; y <- cumsum(sl * sin(hd)) / 1000
map_par()
plot(x, y, type = "n", asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     main = "A two-mode walk: no power law anywhere")
segments(head(x, -1), head(y, -1), x[-1], y[-1], lwd = 2,
         col = c(teal, rust)[state[-1]])
points(x[state == 1], y[state == 1], pch = 16, cex = 0.8, col = teal)
legend("bottomright", c("searching", "travelling"), col = c(teal, rust), lwd = 3,
       bty = "n", cex = 1.3)
```

[Figure produced with own R code · simulated data]{.credit}


Grey: one exponential. Gold: a true power law. Red: two exponential modes, no
power law anywhere — yet heavy-tailed enough that a power law beats a single
exponential by thousands of AIC units.

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
You fit an exponential and a power law to 2,000 step lengths by maximum
likelihood. The power law wins by more than 2,000 AIC units. What have you
shown?

- [ ] The animal performs a Lévy walk
- [ ] The animal optimises its search
- [x] The step lengths are heavy-tailed — which a mixture of two behaviours can produce just as well
- [ ] The exponential model failed to converge

::: {.quiz-feedback}
In the practical you will generate exactly this result from a mixture of two
*exponential* distributions — a short-step mode and a long-step mode, and no
power law anywhere. The power law wins decisively anyway.

A fit tells you about the **shape** of a distribution. It cannot tell you
which **process** generated it. To argue for a Lévy strategy you would need to
rule out composite walks — for instance by showing that the long steps do not
belong to a distinct behavioural state (Session 8).
:::
:::

# 6 · Simulation as a hypothesis test {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## The recipe

::: {.incremental}
1. Choose a **statistic** that captures your question — net displacement,
   radius of gyration, time to reach water
2. Choose a **null process** that lacks the mechanism you are testing — a CRW
   with the animal's own step and turn distributions, but no memory
3. **Simulate** it many times; compute the statistic each time
4. Locate the observed value in the simulated distribution
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
The null must match the animal in everything **except** the mechanism. A null
with the wrong step lengths is a straw man, and rejecting it proves nothing.
:::

---

## The recipe, applied

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| cache: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-align: center
buffalo <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier, t = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)
trk <- make_track(buffalo, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736)
rg <- function(x, y) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2 + (y - mean(y))^2)) / 1000

null_test <- function(animal, n_sim = 300) {           # exactly as in the practical
  hourly <- trk |> filter(id == animal) |>
    track_resample(rate = lubridate::hours(1), tolerance = lubridate::minutes(10)) |>
    filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)
  st <- hourly |> steps_by_burst() |> filter(sl_ > 0, sl_ < 10000)
  g  <- fit_distr(st$sl_, "gamma")
  vm <- fit_distr(st$ta_[!is.na(st$ta_)], "vonmises")
  longest <- hourly |> filter(burst_ == names(which.max(table(burst_))))
  n <- nrow(longest)
  sim <- replicate(n_sim, {
    d <- simulate_crw(n, shape = g$params$shape, scale = g$params$scale, kappa = vm$params$kappa)
    rg(d$x, d$y)
  })
  list(id = animal, days = round(n / 24), obs = rg(longest$x_, longest$y_), sim = sim)
}
set.seed(7)
tests <- lapply(unique(trk$id), null_test)
show  <- tests[sapply(tests, `[[`, "id") %in% c("Gabs", "Toni")]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); slide_par()
for (k in show) {
  pct <- round(100 * mean(k$sim < k$obs))
  hist(k$sim, breaks = 30, col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.5), border = "white",
       xlim = range(k$sim, k$obs), xlab = "Radius of gyration (km)", ylab = "Simulated CRWs",
       main = sprintf("%s: %d days, percentile %d", k$id, k$days, pct))
  abline(v = k$obs, lwd = 5, col = rust)
}
```

[Figure produced with own R code · data: Kruger buffalo, Getz et al. (Movebank); null model simulated]{.credit}


Grey-green: 300 CRWs with the buffalo's own steps and turns. Red line: the
buffalo. Only the longer track is clearly more confined than its null.

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
You test whether a buffalo is range-resident by comparing its radius of
gyration with 300 CRWs built from its own steps and turns. For a 36-day track
it sits at the 73rd percentile; for a 157-day track of another buffalo, the
1st. What is the most important lesson?

- [ ] Only the second buffalo is range-resident
- [ ] The test is broken
- [x] Confinement is detectable only when the track is much longer than the time needed to cross the range
- [ ] More simulations would make the first test significant

::: {.quiz-feedback}
These are real results for the Kruger buffalo. Over a month, a resident and a
random walker cover similar ground: the resident has not yet had time to hit
the edges of its range. Only over months does the random walker keep spreading
while the resident stays put.

More simulations only sharpen the null distribution; they do not add
information about the animal. This is the **tracking duration versus
occupation timescale** problem — and exactly what the variogram in Session 6
diagnoses.
:::
:::

## Recap

::: {.incremental}
- Simulation replaces the replication nature will not give you
- Uncorrelated walk: MSD ∝ t. CRW: ballistic at short scales, diffusive at long
- Bias adds drift, which always wins eventually; a bias towards home
  **creates** a home range
- Power-law step lengths are not evidence of a Lévy strategy
- A simulation null must match the animal in everything but the mechanism —
  and has power only if the track is long enough
:::
